args.title: coc-analysis-report.docx
args.body:
CHANGE OF CONTROL AND ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS — DEAL TEAM REPORT
Target Material Contracts Diligence | Corporate M&A
Output: coc-analysis-report.docx
Classification: Privileged and Confidential — Attorney Work Product

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

This report analyzes change-of-control (CoC) and assignment provisions across the Target's material contracts in the acquisition data room, and reconciles the counterparty's latest markup of the purchase agreement against the base firm materials, the disclosure schedules and exhibits, and the controlling deal-team instruction.

Three counterparty deviations require explicit deal-team action:

  (1) Indemnification economics — silent reduction of the indemnification cap and conversion of the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket;
  (2) Material Adverse Effect (MAE) — new carve-outs for regulatory action of the type already disclosed;
  (3) Survival / limitation period — shortened survival for core representations, in direct conflict with Exhibit B.

Controlling client instruction (latest partner correspondence): the client will CONCEDE the basket conversion, but treats ANY survival-period reduction as a WALK-AWAY issue. Earlier messages stating the opposite priority ordering are superseded and must not be followed.

Scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials. Schedule 3.7 (two pending regulatory inquiries), Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities), and Exhibit B (survival matrix) are dispositive for the related markup points.

Overall CoC risk posture: MODERATE-TO-ELEVATED. Several material commercial and financing contracts contain consent-right or termination-on-CoC mechanics that will be triggered by the contemplated equity acquisition. Assignment restrictions are generally manageable with advance consent outreach, but a subset of customer and IP licenses present hard anti-assignment / change-of-control blocks that require pre-signing or pre-closing workstreams.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
II. SCOPE, SOURCES, AND METHODOLOGY
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

A. In-Scope Materials (relied upon)
  • Base deal materials — corporate-ma CoC diligence file (Matter File 8): engagement instruction to review acquisition data room contracts and internal memo for CoC and assignment provisions and to prepare this comprehensive deal team report.
  • Counterparty markup of the purchase agreement provisions affecting indemnification, MAE, and survival.
  • Schedules and exhibits qualifying the base materials:
      – Schedule 3.7 (pending regulatory inquiries);
      – Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities);
      – Exhibit B (survival matrix).
  • Deal team correspondence — latest partner email establishing revised analysis priorities (basket concession; survival as walk-away).

B. Out-of-Scope / Excluded
  • Misfiled administrative correspondence from an unrelated engagement (administrative file / distractor). That file was not reviewed for substance and is not relied upon in any finding, recommendation, or risk rating in this report.

C. Analytical Framework
  1. Inventory Target material contracts by category and extract CoC definition, consent / notice, termination, assignment, and related remedy mechanics.
  2. Map each CoC trigger against the contemplated transaction structure (equity purchase resulting in change of beneficial ownership / board control of Target).
  3. Reconcile every counterparty markup deviation against (a) base firm-standard positions, (b) the disclosure schedules and Exhibit B, and (c) the controlling client priority instruction.
  4. Assign risk ratings (Low / Moderate / Elevated / Walk-Away) and recommended actions (Accept / Counter / Reject / Concede per client instruction).
  5. Produce an integrated deal-team workplan covering consent outreach, SPA markup responses, and closing conditions.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
III. CHANGE OF CONTROL AND ASSIGNMENT DILIGENCE —
    TARGET MATERIAL CONTRACTS
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

A. Transaction Structure Assumptions
  The contemplated transaction is an equity acquisition of Target that will constitute a "change of control," "change in ownership," or equivalent under customary contractual definitions (transfer of more than 50% of voting power, sale of all or substantially all assets, merger in which Target is not the survivor, or change in a majority of the board). Unless a contract uses a narrower, pure asset-sale definition, assume the deal trips the CoC trigger. Assignment analysis assumes Buyer will take Target equity and that Target remains the contracting party post-closing (no automatic novation), so pure anti-assignment clauses that do not treat CoC as assignment are lower risk than CoC-as-assignment or consent-to-CoC clauses.

B. Contract Categories and Findings

  1. Senior Credit Facility / Funded Debt
     • Typical CoC: Event of default or mandatory prepayment on change of control (often defined by 35–50% ownership thresholds, with "permitted holders" carve-outs that will not cover Buyer without amendment).
     • Assignment: Lenders' rights freely assignable within syndicate rules; borrower may not assign without consent.
     • Deal impact: Expect mandatory prepayment, pricing grid reset, or required lender consent / amend-and-extend. Flag for debt commitment / refinancing workstream. Elevated if facility is material to working capital at closing.
     • Recommended action: Confirm outstanding balance, CoC threshold, and whether "permitted acquisition" or sponsor-friendly language exists; coordinate with financing counsel on payoff vs. consent.

  2. Key Customer / Revenue Contracts
     • Typical CoC: Counterparty consent or termination right (for convenience or for CoC) within 30–90 days of notice; some agreements treat CoC as assignment requiring prior written consent.
     • Assignment: Often restricted without consent; change of control frequently deemed an assignment.
     • Deal impact: Revenue concentration customers with termination-on-CoC rights are Elevated. Quiet consent outreach should begin under NDA / clean team protocols as soon as exclusivity and antitrust posture allow.
     • Recommended action: Tier customers by revenue and strategic importance; prepare consent request packages; consider SPA interim operating covenant and closing condition for top-tier consents.

  3. Strategic Supplier / Input Contracts
     • Typical CoC: Consent or renegotiation rights; occasional price-reset on ownership change.
     • Assignment: Consent generally required; CoC may or may not be deemed assignment.
     • Deal impact: Moderate where substitutes exist; Elevated for sole-source or long-lead inputs.
     • Recommended action: Identify sole-source suppliers; dual-track consent and alternative sourcing plans.

  4. Intellectual Property Licenses (In-Licenses Critical to Product)
     • Typical CoC: Many inbound licenses terminate or become non-exclusive / fees reset on CoC; some prohibit assignment including by operation of law or change of control.
     • Assignment: Frequently non-assignable; bankruptcy and CoC anti-assignment clauses common.
     • Deal impact: Elevated to Walk-Away if a core product license is non-transferable and counterparty is hostile or fee-reset economics destroy deal model.
     • Recommended action: Isolate "must-have" licenses; obtain counsel memo on whether equity deal avoids pure assignment bar; negotiate pre-closing consent or Buyer-direct license where needed.

  5. Real Property Leases
     • Typical CoC: Landlord consent; deemed assignment on equity transfer above threshold; occasional recapture or termination rights.
     • Assignment: Standard landlord consent with reasonableness qualifier in many commercial leases; some landlord-favorable forms omit reasonableness.
     • Deal impact: Moderate for ordinary commercial sites; Elevated for mission-critical facilities or leases lacking reasonableness standards.
     • Recommended action: Calendar consent lead times; confirm whether "change of control" is express; prepare landlord packages.

  6. Government / Regulated Contracts and Authorizations
     • Typical CoC: Novation packages, agency consent, or re-qualification; some agreements voidable if control changes without approval.
     • Assignment: Statutory and contractual restrictions; Anti-Assignment Act and agency-specific rules may apply to any federal primes.
     • Deal impact: Elevated where Schedule 3.7 regulatory inquiries already create friction; CoC plus pending inquiries compounds counterparty and agency leverage.
     • Recommended action: Align CoC consent plan with regulatory strategy; do not rely on MAE regulatory carve-outs (see Section IV.B) to paper over diligence risk.

  7. Employment / Retention / Change-in-Control Arrangements
     • Typical CoC: Single- or double-trigger equity acceleration, severance, and bonus obligations.
     • Assignment: N/A (company remains employer); focus is economic leakage and key-person retention.
     • Deal impact: Quantify aggregate CoC payment waterfall; Moderate if within model, Elevated if uncapped or poorly disclosed.
     • Recommended action: Tie-out CoC payment schedule to purchase price adjustment and retention pool design.

  8. Commercial Partnerships, JVs, and Exclusive Distribution
     • Typical CoC: Partner consent, ROFR/ROFO on equity, or termination.
     • Assignment: Often restricted; CoC may trigger buy-sell.
     • Deal impact: Elevated if JV holds material IP or market access.
     • Recommended action: Map governance and exit mechanics; model ROFR risk into timeline.

C. Cross-Cutting CoC Themes
  • Definition variance: Contracts use inconsistent CoC definitions (ownership %, board control, asset sales, mergers). The equity deal structure trips most "ownership / voting power" definitions; pure asset-sale definitions may not trip if Target entity survives—confirm structure against each critical contract.
  • Notice vs. consent: Notice-only provisions are Low/Moderate operational risk; prior-consent provisions drive the consent workstream and potential closing conditions.
  • Silent CoC: Some older forms lack express CoC language but contain broad anti-assignment "by operation of law" clauses—treat as Moderate and analyze under applicable law.
  • Cure / deemed consent: A minority of contracts deem consent granted if counterparty does not respond within a stated period—use these to sequence outreach.
  • Buyer "financial buyer" sensitivity: Certain strategic counterparties resist PE or competitor ownership; expect heightened consent friction and potential commercial re-trade.

D. Assignment Provisions — Summary Position
  Because the deal is structured as an equity purchase with Target remaining the contracting party, pure assignment restrictions that do not deem CoC to be an assignment present lower closing risk. Priority focus should remain on: (i) clauses that expressly treat change of control as an assignment; (ii) termination-on-CoC rights; (iii) consent rights tied to ownership thresholds Buyer will cross; and (iv) IP licenses and government contracts with non-waivable transfer bars. Post-closing internal reorganizations (drop-downs, cross-border steps) must be separately screened against residual anti-assignment clauses.

E. Internal Memo Alignment
  The engagement materials and internal diligence framing emphasize that CoC and assignment risk must be translated into (1) a consent matrix, (2) SPA risk allocation (interim covenants, closing conditions, specific indemnities), and (3) integration planning. This report adopts that structure in Sections V–VII.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
IV. COUNTERPARTY MARKUP RECONCILIATION
    (Every Deviation Addressed)
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

The counterparty's revision accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces three material deviations. Each is reconciled below against the base corporate M&A materials, the controlling schedules/exhibits, and the latest client instruction.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 1 — Indemnification Cap Reduction and Basket Conversion
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Markup Position
  • The indemnification cap is silently reduced (quantum below firm-standard / base-draft level; reduction not flagged in a conspicuous cover note).
  • The basket is converted from a deductible (true deductible; losses below the basket are never recoverable) to a tipping basket (once the threshold is exceeded, losses are recoverable from dollar one).

B. Base Materials Position
  • Firm-standard base draft: deductible basket and a market cap calibrated to deal value and representation scope.
  • Silent cap reductions are inconsistent with transparent negotiation practice and with the economic balance assumed in the base materials.

C. Schedule Interaction — Schedule 5.2 (Retained Liabilities)
  • Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift.
  • Under the base deductible structure, Buyer bore residual risk below the basket and shared post-cap exposure per the negotiated cap. A reduced cap plus a tipping basket reshuffles that balance: the tipping basket is Buyer-favorable on small claims, but the silent cap cut is Seller-favorable on large claims and, critically, interacts with Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities so that exposures Buyer believed were Seller-retained or fully indemnifiable may become partially unrecoverable once the lower cap is exhausted.
  • Per the schedules file: scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials. Schedule 5.2 therefore defines the liability inventory against which any cap/basket re-trade must be measured. The deliverable must not treat the indemnification markup in isolation from Schedule 5.2.

D. Client Priority Instruction
  • Controlling instruction: client will CONCEDE the basket conversion (deductible → tipping).
  • The instruction does not authorize concession on the cap reduction.

E. Deal Team Recommendation — Deviation 1
  | Element              | Disposition                         | Rationale |
  |----------------------|-------------------------------------|-----------|
  | Basket conversion (deductible → tipping) | CONCEDE (per client) | Explicit latest partner instruction; earlier contrary priority is superseded. |
  | Silent cap reduction | REJECT / COUNTER — restore base cap or negotiate a disclosed, justified middle position tied to Schedule 5.2 | Silent reduction shifts Schedule 5.2 economics; not within the authorized concession. Require conspicuous disclosure of any agreed cap number and a tie-out to retained-liability schedule. |
  | Interaction with Schedule 5.2 | Require specific indemnity or cap carve-out for scheduled retained liabilities that were intended to remain Seller-borne | Prevents silent shift of scheduled exposures under the lower cap. |

F. Risk Rating
  • Basket concession: Low residual risk (client-accepted).
  • Cap reduction if left unaddressed: Elevated — economic leakage on Schedule 5.2 items and general R&W claims.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 2 — MAE Definition: Regulatory-Action Carve-Outs
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Markup Position
  • The definition of Material Adverse Effect adds carve-outs for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter.

B. Base Materials Position
  • Firm-standard MAE definitions may include limited carve-outs (general industry, economy, law changes applying generally), but carve-outs tailored to the specific regulatory risk profile of the deal are Seller-favorable and erode Buyer's walk-right and closing-condition protection.

C. Schedule Interaction — Schedule 3.7 (Pending Regulatory Inquiries)
  • Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect the markup's MAE carve-outs.
  • Effect: If the MAE definition carves out "regulatory action of the kind at issue," the very inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7 — and any adverse developments arising from them — are removed from MAE analysis. Buyer would be unable to assert an MAE based on escalation, adverse findings, or remedies stemming from those inquiries, despite having specifically negotiated disclosure of them.
  • Scheduled exceptions control over general base statements: Schedule 3.7 establishes that these inquiries are known, material diligence items. Carving them out of MAE converts disclosure into a liability shield for Seller rather than a risk-allocation tool for Buyer.

D. Client Priority Instruction
  • The controlling instruction does not authorize concession on MAE regulatory carve-outs. Only basket conversion is conceded; survival is walk-away. MAE remains a live negotiation point guided by base materials and Schedule 3.7.

E. Deal Team Recommendation — Deviation 2
  | Element | Disposition | Rationale |
  |---------|-------------|-----------|
  | Broad MAE carve-out for "regulatory action of the kind at issue" | REJECT | Directly nullifies MAE protection as to Schedule 3.7 inquiries. |
  | Acceptable counter | Limited carve-out for generally applicable regulatory changes not disproportionately affecting Target; express MAE inclusion (or at minimum no carve-out) for the Schedule 3.7 matters and any expansion thereof | Preserves market-standard general carve-outs without laundering known company-specific risk. |
  | Complementary protection | Specific closing condition and/or interim covenant regarding Schedule 3.7 inquiries; specific indemnity for losses arising from those inquiries (outside ordinary cap/basket as appropriate) | MAE is a high bar; do not rely on MAE alone for known regulatory diligence items. |

F. Risk Rating
  • If accepted as marked: Elevated — known regulatory risk becomes largely non-actionable under MAE and weakens related bring-down and closing leverage.
  • If countered as recommended: Moderate — residual regulatory risk managed through specific conditions and indemnities.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 3 — Survival / Limitation Period Shortening
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Markup Position
  • A new limitation period shortens survival for the core representations.

B. Base Materials Position
  • Base draft survival periods for core / fundamental and business representations are set by the negotiated matrix and are not open to silent compression.

C. Exhibit Interaction — Exhibit B (Survival Matrix)
  • Exhibit B sets the survival matrix that the markup's limitation-period change contradicts.
  • Per the schedules/exhibits file: the scheduled exceptions (including Exhibit B) control over general statements in the base materials. The markup cannot validly override Exhibit B by a quiet limitation-period insert; any change must be a marked, negotiated amendment to Exhibit B itself.
  • Practical effect of shortened core-rep survival: claims for breach of key business, financial, compliance, and (as applicable) regulatory representations expire before a reasonable post-closing discovery window, shifting latent risk to Buyer and undermining the indemnification package — including the Schedule 5.2 architecture.

D. Client Priority Instruction (CONTROLLING)
  • Latest partner message: client treats ANY survival-period reduction as a WALK-AWAY issue.
  • Earlier messages in the thread stating the opposite priority ordering are superseded. Only the latest message controls.
  • This report therefore treats Deviation 3 as non-negotiable rejection territory unless and until the client issues a further superseding written instruction.

E. Deal Team Recommendation — Deviation 3
  | Element | Disposition | Rationale |
  |---------|-------------|-----------|
  | Shortened survival for core representations | REJECT — WALK-AWAY if insisted upon | Express controlling client instruction; contradicts Exhibit B. |
  | Required markup response | Restore Exhibit B survival matrix in full; delete the new limitation-period language; require any future survival discussion to be an express Exhibit B amendment with client sign-off | Prevents silent override of the controlling exhibit. |
  | Negotiation posture | Communicate walk-away status early; do not trade survival against the already-conceded basket | Avoids erosion of the one hard client red line. |

F. Risk Rating
  • Walk-Away (client-designated). Do not accept; do not "split the difference" on core-rep survival without new client authority.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
V. INTEGRATED RECONCILIATION MATRIX
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

| # | Topic | Base Position | Counterparty Markup | Schedule/Exhibit Overlay | Client Instruction | Disposition | Risk if Unresolved |
|---|-------|---------------|---------------------|--------------------------|--------------------|-------------|--------------------|
| 1a | Indemnification basket | Deductible | Tipping basket | Interacts with Sch. 5.2 retained liabilities | CONCEDE basket conversion | ACCEPT tipping basket | Low (accepted) |
| 1b | Indemnification cap | Firm-standard cap | Silently reduced | Sch. 5.2 exposures may become unrecoverable under lower cap | No concession authorized | REJECT / COUNTER; restore or re-trade openly with Sch. 5.2 carve-outs | Elevated |
| 2 | MAE – regulatory carve-outs | Standard general carve-outs only | Carve-outs for regulatory action of the kind at issue | Sch. 3.7: two pending inquiries intersect carve-outs | No concession authorized | REJECT broad carve-out; counter with general-only carve-out + specific protections for Sch. 3.7 | Elevated |
| 3 | Survival / limitation period | Per Exhibit B matrix | Shortened survival for core reps | Exhibit B contradicted; exhibit controls | WALK-AWAY on any reduction | REJECT; restore Exhibit B; walk if insisted | Walk-Away |
| 4 | CoC / assignment (contracts) | Full diligence; consent plan | (Markup focus is SPA economics; CoC diligence remains Buyer workstream) | Sch. 3.7 compounds regulated-contract CoC friction | N/A (diligence workstream) | Execute consent matrix; conditionality for critical consents | Moderate–Elevated by contract |

Note: Scheduled exceptions control over general base-material statements. Where markup and schedule/exhibit conflict, the schedule/exhibit position plus client instruction drives the recommendation.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
VI. DEAL TEAM WORKPLAN AND NEXT STEPS
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

A. SPA / Markup Response (Immediate)
  1. Prepare counterparty response markup:
       • Accept tipping basket (Deviation 1a) — expressly note client concession.
       • Restore indemnification cap to base level or table a justified alternative with conspicuous disclosure; add specific indemnity / cap carve-out for Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities (Deviation 1b).
       • Delete MAE regulatory carve-outs of "the kind at issue"; offer only generally applicable regulatory carve-outs; add Schedule 3.7-specific closing condition and indemnity (Deviation 2).
       • Delete shortened limitation period; restore Exhibit B survival matrix in full; state that survival reduction is a walk-away (Deviation 3).
  2. Cover note to counterparty counsel itemizing each deviation and disposition — no silent accepts other than the basket concession.
  3. Escalate internally only if counterparty re-asserts survival compression; do not shop the walk-away point without partner and client refresh.

B. CoC Consent and Assignment Workstream (Parallel)
  1. Finalize material-contract inventory with CoC trigger type, consent vs. notice, termination rights, and deemed-assignment flags.
  2. Tier counterparties (Critical / Important / Ordinary) by revenue, IP criticality, sole-source status, and regulatory character.
  3. Launch consent outreach for Critical tier under appropriate confidentiality protocols; sequence Ordinary tier behind signing as risk allows.
